title: Faith and reason
hookLine: Christians have long held both are gifts from the same God

lines: THE MIND, A DOOR TO CLOSE?
cards: A Bible study, a Tuesday night, folding chairs in a circle. A teenager in the back raises her hand and asks what others have been sitting on: if I keep asking questions, does that mean I don't have enough faith?
It's an old worry, that thinking hard is the opposite of believing, that the mind is a door you close before you kneel. A line of Christian thinkers answers that worry with a no.
Faith and reason, they say, come from the same God, and he isn't afraid of either one.

teach.b: Asked for the great commandment, Jesus answers: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind." The mind is on the list. Thinking is one of the ways love is given.
Then Isaiah, where God opens what sounds like a case at law: "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD." An invitation to talk it through.
In Acts, Paul preaches in a town called Berea, and the people there "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so."
They checked the apostle against the scrolls, and the text calls them more noble for it.
A letter of Peter asks Christians to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." A reason, and a gentle one.
Anselm of Canterbury described his work as faith seeking understanding: faith goes first, then goes looking.
Pope John Paul II began a letter on this subject with a picture: faith and reason are like two wings, and the human spirit rises on both toward the truth. Christians weigh the two wings differently.

Some put trust in how far reason can reach toward God on its own. Others stress how easily a human mind wanders, and lean harder on what God reveals. But in these texts, nobody is asked to switch the mind off.
A bird with one wing doesn't get far.

how: Christians bring faith and reason together in Bible study groups, catechism classes, theology and apologetics; Catholic teaching in particular has written at length on how the two work together, and Protestant and Orthodox churches each have their own traditions of careful thinking about faith.

o: believing first, then never asking again
trust and careful thinking, as gifts of one God
two rivals, where one must always win

games.q: faith and reason — tap the pairs.

s: in Acts, the people who checked Paul's preaching are scolded
the Bereans searched the scriptures to see whether those things were so, and Acts calls them more noble.
Jesus names the mind as one way to love God
heart, soul and mind, in the great commandment in Matthew.
the letter of Peter asks for a reason given harshly
it asks for a reason of the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear.

games.q: you live in Berea, and a traveling preacher named Paul says the scriptures point to Jesus. what do you do?
o: believe it at once, no questions.
listen gladly, then search the scriptures to check.
games.why: the Bereans received the word with readiness of mind and searched the scriptures daily to see if it was so. Acts calls them more noble for checking.

practice: Pick one thing you hold to be true: that people are mostly good, that prayer matters, that there's nothing after death.
Ask it three plain questions: where did I first get this, why do I still hold it, and what would I say if a friend asked why?
You don't have to change it; look at it in good light, the way the Bereans unrolled the scrolls, and if you pray, ask for an honest mind.

wordCard.voice: Faith and reason. Trust and careful thinking, gifts of the same God, these thinkers say, meant to fly together.

orig.note: Greek: mind, understanding — the word behind "with all thy mind" in Matthew 22:37.

carryVoice: Your line: two wings. The Bereans were called noble for checking the scrolls. Go gently.
